title: The Drove Road

where.detail: a shepherds' fold on the drove road round the north shore of the tarn, across the water from Coldmere

time: the first day off the mountain, from the first miles to dusk
last_beat: Across the tarn the column's fires came out on Coldmere's green, and Rae pointed with the goad at the biggest light, her uncle's inn, where he would be pouring for them.

people.did: Walked the first miles at Hob's head to Maelis's stone, watching every rise for the banner; knew Aldric at the head of the column and wanted to stand on the Holloway and meet him; owned that he had decided before anyone spoke, and gave Rae the road.
people.now: At a shepherds' fold on the drove road round the tarn, with the company, the column's fires across the water at Coldmere.

facts.fact: He walked the first miles of the Holloway at the ox's head, the stick in one hand.
facts.evidence: So he walked at Hob's head with one hand on the yoke and the stick in the other

facts.fact: He owned that he had decided to meet the banner before anyone spoke, and left the road to Rae.
facts.evidence: "Your road," Darrow said.

facts.fact: He knew Aldric at the head of the column by his seat on a horse.
facts.evidence: That's Aldric.

people.did: Told him she had told the mare her name; took the cart off the Holloway onto the drove road round the tarn rather than drive it into a Lance on the march, and argued it out loud; waited for his word before she drove on.
people.now: At the fold on the north shore of the tarn, looking across at Coldmere, where the column has stopped on the green and her uncle keeps the inn at the water's edge.

facts.fact: She told the grey mare her name at the dealer's, as she said she would.
facts.evidence: In her ear, at the dealer's, the morning I went down.

facts.fact: She would not drive her cart into a Lance on the march: a Lance on the march takes a cart.
facts.evidence: This is my road, and I'm not driving it into him so you can see his face.

facts.fact: Her uncle keeps the inn whose light is the biggest in Coldmere, at the water's edge.
facts.evidence: "That's my uncle's," she said.

people.did: Rode the tailboard, ordered that sheep not be counted separately, backed the carter, and called the fold the finest inn in the Lowmarch.
people.now: At the fold on the drove road, asking where they keep the beer.

facts.fact: He backed the carter over the banner: a Lance's outriders have eyes.
facts.evidence: but they've outriders, and outriders have eyes

people.did: Let him walk to the next milestone and no further, then put him back on the tailboard.
people.now: With the company at the fold on the drove road.

facts.fact: She let him walk the Holloway to a milestone, then had him ride.
facts.evidence: To the next stone. Then you ride, and you don't argue.

people.did: Counted everything on the road, sheep included until Hollis forbade it; counted the column at forty-six and its cart; began to count the stars.
people.now: Flat on her back on the cart at the fold, counting the sky.

facts.fact: She counted the column on the Holloway: forty-six riders and the Confessor's cart.
facts.evidence: Forty-six. Their cart. His cart.

facts.fact: On the mountain the sky had mostly been cloud; at the fold she began to count the stars.
facts.evidence: Nobody's ever tried.

people.did: Ranged ahead on the road and came back twice to report nothing.
people.now: With the company at the fold on the drove road.

codex.name: The drove road
codex.text: A walled track that leaves the Holloway above Coldmere and runs north round the far side of the tarn: the carter's road round a Lance on the march (Ch 5 Sc 1).

fired.evidence: In her ear, at the dealer's, the morning I went down.

season: clear cold after the first snow, on the road below the mountain

now.against: A Lance on the march and the Confessor's cart, camped on Coldmere's green across the tarn.
now.next: Round the tarn by the drove road, to come at Coldmere from the north.

title: Across the Water

where.detail: on the fold wall above the tarn at the shepherds' fold, across the water from Coldmere

time: the first night off the mountain, after dark
last_beat: Her shoulder stayed against his, and, looking across the water and not at him, Rae asked her one question of the night: what he had been going to say to Aldric on the road.

people.did: Took Rae a cup from the kettle on the fold wall with no light, asked about the man pouring for the column, would not tell her it would be all right, and offered to go round Coldmere rather than put her uncle to it.
people.now: On the fold wall beside Rae, with Ash across their feet, her question waiting: what he was going to say to Aldric.

facts.fact: He told Rae they would go round Coldmere rather than put her uncle to it.
facts.evidence: If it isn't good for the inn,

people.did: Kept the fold dark from the far shore; told him about her uncle and his taproom, and that she went out the back the night the list was read without asking him; made her one question of the night his: what he was going to say to Aldric.
people.now: On the fold wall above the tarn, watching her uncle's door across the water, her shoulder against Darrow's.

facts.fact: Her uncle keeps the only inn in Coldmere; everything on the Holloway goes through his taproom, and he pours for all of them and forgets none of it.
facts.evidence: He pours for all of them, and he listens to all of them, and he forgets none of it.

facts.fact: Her uncle poured for the reader the night the list was read in his taproom, between the names.
facts.evidence: filled the reader's cup between the names

facts.fact: The night the list was read she went out the back to the House's cart without asking her uncle, the first thing she had not asked him.
facts.evidence: That was the first thing I didn't.

facts.fact: She does not know whether her uncle will give them up: he does what is good for the inn.
facts.evidence: He'll do what's good for the inn. He always has.

people.did: Built the fire inside the shepherds' hut so it would not show across the tarn, on Rae's word.
people.now: In the shepherds' hut with the kettle.

people.did: Lay down across Darrow's and Rae's feet on the fold wall.
people.now: Across their feet on the fold wall.

now.against: A Lance and the Confessor's cart camped on Coldmere's green; her uncle pouring for them.
now.next: Round the tarn by the drove road.

title: The Better Seat

where.detail: on the fold wall above the tarn at the shepherds' fold, Coldmere dark across the water

time: the first night off the mountain, late
last_beat: Rae put the empty cup into his hands and said she does not open what she carries; across the water the inn's door shut for the night, and in the hut Hollis went on singing.

people.did: Answered Rae's question: first that he missed Aldric; then, with the hut door shut on Hollis, that Aldric's horse was already turned one heartbeat before the warmth went, that he fears it was known and does not want it to be true, and that he wanted to ask Aldric to his face.
people.now: On the fold wall beside Rae, holding the empty cup; he has told one person what he saw from the water.

facts.fact: He told Rae he had wanted to ask Aldric to his face whether he knew, and to watch him answer.
facts.evidence: I wanted to stand in front of him and say, *Did you know?* and watch it while he answered.

facts.fact: He believes somebody knew the ford was coming, and does not want it to be Aldric.
facts.evidence: And I don't want it to be true.

people.did: Called his first answer light, heard the rest, told him a face shows what a man fears and not what he did, and said what he told her is carried and unopened.
people.now: On the fold wall above the dark tarn, keeping what he told her.

facts.fact: She keeps the faces of everyone she has brought to the foot of the Steps and taken down again.
facts.evidence: Every man I've brought to the foot of those stairs, and every one I took down again.

facts.fact: She holds that a face tells what a man is afraid of, not what he did.
facts.evidence: A face tells you what a man's afraid of. It's no good at all for what he did.

facts.fact: She does not open what she carries.
facts.evidence: I don't open what I carry.

people.did: Sang one of the Sixth's songs to the kettle in the shepherds' hut, the verses nobody should hear.
people.now: In the shepherds' hut, singing.

fired.evidence: I wanted to stand in front of him and say, *Did you know?* and watch it while he answered.

title: Above Every Other

where.detail: in the lee of a field wall past a drove-road hamlet, the reeve's lantern at the barred gate

time: the second day off the mountain, from noon to dusk
last_beat: The reeve held his lantern up to the bars of the field gate, past Rae to the faces round the fire, and stopped on Darrow's: who rides on the Thorne cart?

people.did: Read his own name at the top of the writ standing up; offered to be put off the cart so Rae could trade, and walked when she refused; faced the reeve's lantern at the gate.
people.now: At the fire behind a field wall past the hamlet, with the reeve at the barred gate asking who rides on the Thorne cart.

facts.fact: The writs now carry his name alone at the top, above every other.
facts.evidence: His name sat alone at the top, in letters a size bigger than the rest

facts.fact: He offered to be put off the cart so the hamlet would sell to Rae.
facts.evidence: Put me off at the next wall,

people.did: Read her own name on the writ, under his, and said plainly what it meant: she is wanted as much as he is and is easier to carry off, and he is not to stand in front of her about it.
people.now: At the fire past the hamlet, named on the writs.

facts.fact: The writs name her too: the Mender Vorne, of Saint Ysolde's, who harbours him.
facts.evidence: the Mender Vorne, of Saint Ysolde's, who harbours him.

facts.fact: She told him not to stand in front of her about the writ.
facts.evidence: Don't go standing in front of me about it. You'll only fall over.

people.did: Was refused at the reeve's door, where she has sold since she could lift a sack; would not put her load down to trade; took the bread a Faithless man brought over the wall.
people.now: At the fire past the hamlet, her custom there spent on the man she carries, the reeve at the gate calling her by name.

facts.fact: She has sold to the hamlet's reeve since she could lift a sack, and his father before him; he would not buy off her cart with the writ on the post.
facts.evidence: Not off that cart, Rae. Not with that on the post.

facts.fact: She would not put her load down because a reeve looked at it.
facts.evidence: And then I'd be a carter who put her load down because a reeve looked at it.

people.did: Found himself third on the writ and took it like a wound; opened the bread.
people.now: At the fire past the hamlet.

facts.fact: On the new writ he is third, under Darrow and the Mender.
facts.evidence: I was second at the bars.

people.did: Read the writ aloud and found him first, alone, above every other.
people.now: At the fire past the hamlet.

facts.fact: She read the writ on the bell-post aloud.
facts.evidence: Wren read it aloud behind him, fast, as she read everything.

codex.name: The bell-post writ
codex.text: A Knight-Confessor's writ under blue wax, nailed at a drove-road hamlet: Darrow's name alone at the top, then the Mender Vorne as his harbourer, then the Ninth and the Sixth man by man (Ch 5 Sc 2).

fired.evidence: His name sat alone at the top, in letters a size bigger than the rest
There's a few of us here heard it. We don't put it on any post.

now.against: Writs on the posts with his name first and the Mender's under it; a frightened hamlet at the gate.
now.next: The reeve wants an answer: who rides on the Thorne cart.

title: A Load Named at a Gate

where.detail: at the fire in the lee of the field wall past the drove-road hamlet, the gate barred and the track dark

time: the second night off the mountain
last_beat: When the others were under their blankets Rae went to see to the oxen, and on the way across the dark the bell at her belt rang once, and she let it.

people.did: Looked to Rae at the gate and let her answer the reeve for her own cart; thanked her across the fire, and ate the half of the bread she gave him.
people.now: Under his blanket by the field wall past the hamlet; the company goes at grey light, and he rides the cart until noon.

facts.fact: He let Rae answer the reeve for her cart, and thanked her for it.
facts.evidence: You answered for me,

people.did: Answered the reeve at the gate: a carter names her load to the one who paid for it, never at a gate; he may say he asked and she would not tell him; the boy only brought bread to a carter he has known all his life.
people.now: Seeing to the oxen in the dark by the field wall; she let the bell at her belt ring.

facts.fact: A carter names her load to the one who paid for it, nobody else, and never at a gate.
facts.evidence: A carter names her load to the one who paid for it. Nobody else, and never at a gate.

facts.fact: She learned the road's law about naming a load from the reeve's father, at his door, when she was nine.
facts.evidence: your father told me why, at your own door, when I was nine

facts.fact: She gave Darrow the larger half of her bread.
facts.evidence: put the larger half on his knee without looking at it

people.did: Counted the men at the gate and the men who went home believing Rae, and marked the one with the fork who can read.
people.now: Asleep by the field wall with one more line in her ledger that she showed nobody.

facts.fact: She marked that the reeve's eldest, the one with the fork, can read and went home unconvinced.
facts.evidence: Men who went home believing her: two.

people.did: Ordered the company gone at grey light before the hamlet's bell, and the leg in the cart until noon.
people.now: By the fire past the hamlet; the company goes at grey light.

facts.fact: She set the leg in the cart until noon on the third day of road.
facts.evidence: The leg's had two days of road; it can have the third in the cart until noon.

people.did: Divided the boy's bread with great care, Rae's share first, and praised her answer as the best lie he ever heard that wasn't one.
people.now: Under his blanket by the field wall.

facts.fact: He called Rae's answer at the gate the best lie he ever heard that wasn't one.
facts.evidence: That," he said, "was the best lie I ever heard that wasn't one.

people.did: Lay with her nose to the gap under the gate, listening to the track.
people.now: On watch at the gate.

fired.evidence: A carter names her load to the one who paid for it. Nobody else, and never at a gate.

now.against: A hamlet that has read the post, and the reeve's eldest who read Darrow's face against it.
now.next: Away at grey light, before the hamlet's bell.

title: From the Belly

where.detail: by the oxen on their short tie in the lee of the field wall past the drove-road hamlet

time: the second night off the mountain, late
last_beat: He went back to his blanket saying the word under his breath and getting it wrong, and behind him, into Hob's neck, Rae laughed again.

people.did: Got up in the cold to help Rae with the oxen, held Hob's head while she took a stone from his foot, talked to the ox like a sergeant, and tried her grandmother's word for stand until Dun stood harder.
people.now: Back at his blanket by the field wall, saying the word for stand under his breath and getting it wrong.

facts.fact: He walked at a horse's head before he could argue.
facts.evidence: I walked at a horse's head before I could argue.

facts.fact: He cannot yet make the catch in the Thornwild word for stand.
facts.evidence: What came out of him was a Lowmarch noise with a hiccup in it

people.did: Went over Hob by feel and took a stone from his near fore; taught Darrow her grandmother's Thornwild word for stand, from the belly, and laughed out loud at him trying it.
people.now: With the oxen on their short tie by the field wall, laughing into Hob's neck.

facts.fact: Her grandmother's Thornwild word for stand is said from the belly, and it stops an ox dead.
facts.evidence: My grandmother's word. It's Thornwild.

facts.fact: Her grandmother had a few dozen Thornwild words, all for oxen.
facts.evidence: She had a few dozen, all for oxen.

facts.fact: She laughed out loud at Darrow trying the word, and covered her mouth after.
facts.evidence: Rae laughed. Not the breath through the nose; out loud, once, into the dark

title: East

where.detail: on the drove road above a turnip field, east of the hamlet

time: the third day off the mountain, from grey light to past noon
last_beat: They let the Hollowed knight walk east over the rise, and Wren, silent since she gave him water, licked her pencil and said she would count them.

people.did: Rode the cart until noon; went down into the turnip field and stood in a Hollowed knight's road, asked his Lance, turned him west and watched him drift back east; remembered the grey figures under the trees at the ford; let him go; asked whether anybody counts them.
people.now: Back on the cart on the drove road, past noon, with a question: how many of them walk east, and does anybody count.

facts.fact: He turned the Hollowed knight west, and the man drifted back east within seven steps.
facts.evidence: by the seventh he was going east again across the rows

facts.fact: He remembered the grey figures under the trees behind the clan carts at the ford.
facts.evidence: a line of grey figures in armour, so still they had not moved even when the river screamed

people.did: Gave the Hollowed knight water without being asked, the way the far cots are given it, and went white doing it; said she would count them.
people.now: On the cart with the ledger open on her knees; she means to count the ones who walk east.

facts.fact: She knows how to make a Hollowed man drink, from the far cots.
facts.evidence: "The far cots."

facts.fact: She has taken on the count of the Hollowed who walk east.
facts.evidence: "I'll count them," she said.

people.did: Put a new sole on Hollis's boot at the tailboard; told Darrow not to take the knight: tied, he would lean east on the rope until it cut him, as every man on her far cots lies turned to the east wall.
people.now: On the cart on the drove road past noon.

facts.fact: She has kept Hollowed men on her cots for thirty years, and every one lies turned toward the east wall when no one is looking.
facts.evidence: every one of them is lying turned toward the east wall

people.did: Told her grandmother's story of the grey country east of the Wend, where they go in the end; home, her grandmother called it.
people.now: Driving the drove road east past the turnip field.

facts.fact: Her grandmother said the grey country east of the Wend is where the Hollowed go in the end, and called it home; Rae never believed it.
facts.evidence: She said that's where they go, in the end. Home, she called it. I never believed a word of it.

people.did: Called to the Hollowed knight in his ford voice and got nothing; said somebody's mother had been shaving him.
people.now: On the cart, out of jokes for the day.

facts.fact: He saw that someone had been keeping the Hollowed knight, shaving him, and grieved it.
facts.evidence: Somebody's been shaving him,

people.did: Walked close to the cart all morning.
people.now: Beside the cart on the drove road.

codex.name: The grey country
codex.text: In a Thornwild grandmother's story, a country east of the Wend where grey people stand among the trees so still the birds sit on them; where the Hollowed go in the end, home, she called it (Ch 5 Sc 3).

fired.evidence: They left the field wall at grey light, before the hamlet's bell had done more than clear its throat

now.against: A Lowmarch where the Hollowed walk east at noon, and writs on the posts.
now.next: Coldmere, from the north, when it is empty of the column.
